# Untitled

Sometimes the narrator imagines that if he simply stood up and walked away from his computer, if he climbed the mountainside to look out over a field of thistles and the sea beyond, he might finally receive the subtle shock or the moment of clarity he keeps searching for. It is there, he thinks—in the ascent, in the open air, in the plain fact of the landscape—that something might break through to him.

But he does not go. Instead he stays fixed to the screen, monitoring microsystems stocks throughout the day, checking and rechecking them with the compulsive hunger of an addicted gambler who cannot look away, always hoping the next glance will show him some profit, some vindication of his waiting.

Each moment arrives overcharged, saturated with feeling. He is suspended between contradictions: a sense of apocalyptic doom pressing down on one side, and on the other a utopian hope for longevity, for a future stretched out endlessly before him. The two live inside him at once, neither yielding to the other.

He asks himself why he can never arrive at any emotional steadiness, why calm remains permanently out of reach. The only equilibrium he can find is a strange one—not the stillness of peace, but the violent balance that comes when extreme and chaotic moods collide and cancel each other out, leaving him briefly suspended in their wreckage.

And in his mind the images begin to merge. The field of thistles on the mountainside blends with the global currencies scrolling across his screen; the physical world and the abstract world of money fold into a single landscape. The natural and the financial become indistinguishable, thistles and currencies growing together in the same imagined ground.

**On the Mountainside, Checking**

He stands where the thistles gather, purple-crowned
and bristling, a whole slope of them nodding
in the dry wind, and he could be anything here—
a shepherd, a monk, a man simply looking
at the way light lifts off the granite
and settles again into shadow. The valley below
is green and blue and going gold at the edges.
He could stay. He could be still.

But his hand goes to his pocket. The small screen
wakes with its cold blue announcement:
microsystems, up an eighth, down a quarter,
the little red and green arrows trembling
like something alive, like the thistles trembling,
like his own pulse trembling in the throat.
Why, he asks the mountain, can't I be as you are—
rooted, indifferent, enduring your weather
without complaint? The thistles do not check
their prices. The stone does not refresh.

And yet he refreshes. He cannot help it.
There is a flock of numbers wheeling in him,
starlings that will not settle on any wire,
and he wonders what it is inside a man
that makes him this way—wired to two worlds,
one that asks nothing and one that asks everything,
one that offers the slow green permission
of grass, of cloud, of the long light thinning,
and one that offers only the next tick,
the next click, the terrible small hope
that something has changed while he wasn't looking.

He watches a hawk. He forgets the hawk.
His mood climbs like the price climbing—
suddenly he is enormous, he is fortunate,
the whole slope is his, the sky is a gift.
Then the number turns and takes him with it,
down into the small hours of himself
where nothing is enough and nothing holds,
where even the beauty of the place accuses him:
*you were here, you were finally here,
and you were somewhere else the entire time.*

What is steadiness? he asks the thistles.
Who among us keeps a level heart?
The market opens and his chest opens with it.
The market closes and he does not close.
He is a weather system of his own making,
high pressure and low pressure chasing each other
across the private country of his face,
and the mountain, which knows nothing of ownership,
holds him anyway, the way it holds the thistles,
the way it holds the light it cannot keep.

He wants transcendence. He wants the eighth of a point.
He wants to be the man who put the screen away
and walked down singing into the ordinary evening.
He wants to know what the next hour brings.
Both wants are true, and neither one will loosen,
and so he stands, refreshing, in the wind,
a small red arrow, a small green arrow,
a soul divided perfectly in half,
asking the indifferent purple flowers
why he cannot, for one moment, simply stay.
outputs.L5:
# May, Whitsuntide, and the Arrival of Spring

May is a month rich with life, warmth, and celebration. As winter's last chill fades away, the world bursts into color, and nature seems to awaken all at once. Trees unfold their fresh green leaves, flowers bloom in gardens and meadows, and the days grow longer and brighter. It is a season that has inspired poets, artists, and ordinary people alike for centuries.

One of the most cherished occasions during this time of year is **Whitsuntide**, the period surrounding Whitsunday (also known as Pentecost). Traditionally observed seven weeks after Easter, Whitsuntide often falls in late May, marking an important moment in the Christian calendar. It commemorates the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles, and historically it was a time of great festivity, church services, and community gatherings.

In many parts of Europe, especially in England and Germany, Whitsuntide **and** the surrounding weeks were filled with colorful customs. Villages would hold fairs, processions, and dances. Homes and churches were decorated with green branches and fresh flowers. Morris dancing, feasting, and games brought communities together in a shared spirit of joy and renewal.

The connection between May and Whitsuntide is a natural one. Both symbolize new beginnings, growth, and the celebration of light after darkness. Whether marked by religious observance or simple enjoyment of the outdoors, this time of year continues to hold a special place in the hearts of many.

As we welcome May **and** the traditions of Whitsuntide, we are reminded of the beauty of renewal, the value of community, and the timeless rhythm of the seasons that connects us to generations past.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental, stream-of-consciousness prose poem about a man checking stock prices on his laptop on a mountainside, mixing financial anxiety with mystical nature imagery and mood swings.
counterfactuals.output:
# Ticker at Altitude

and the pines don't care about my portfolio, they just *stand there* being ancient while the little red numbers bleed down the screen —3.4% —4.1% and somewhere a marmot whistles like it knows something I don't, like it's front-running the whole granite economy of this place—

green now, *green*, the market breathes in and I breathe with it, oxygen thin at nine thousand feet but my lungs full of NASDAQ, full of hope, the sun cracking gold over the ridgeline like a bull run made of actual light, and I am *rich*, I am the richest man on this rock, I could buy this mountain—

no.

the wind turns, the number turns, the clouds come in gray as margin calls and I am nothing, I am a decimal point shivering in a fleece jacket, the granite indifferent, the lichen slow-growing at a yield no human patience could survive—

but look how the light does that, does *that thing* through the needles, dappling, the price of nothing, the P/E ratio of a hawk riding thermals with zero overhead, all profit, all glide—

my thumb refreshes. the cosmos refreshes. somewhere the Fed speaks and here a creek keeps its own liquidity, its own cold running currency downhill toward a sea that never checks the close—

and I want to close the laptop, I *want* to, want to be the marmot, want to be lichen, want the long slow compounding of stone, but the numbers pull me back down the mountain by a wire in my chest, red green red green like a heartbeat that isn't mine, that belongs to a server farm in Virginia humming in the dark while up here the first star ignites, uncorrelated, un-hedged, spending its light for free—

and I don't know if I'm rich. I don't know if I'm ruined. the mountain doesn't file quarterly. the mountain doesn't blink.

I put my hand on the cold rock and for one second

the ticker

*stops*.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, run-on lyrical passage set on May 23rd 2010 (Whitsuntide) featuring thistles, hawks, and microsystems stocks, exploring themes of instability, chaos moods, and negative theology.
counterfactuals.output: On the twenty-third of May, that Whitsun morning of two thousand ten when the tongues of fire were supposed to descend but descended instead as a static crackle over the ticker where Microsystems stock convulsed and sold itself short against its own shadow, the thistles came up purple through the cracked commons, insolent, spiked, indifferent to Pentecost, and I watched the hawks wheel their slow negative gyres above the ring roads like question marks God refused to straighten, and everything shook, the markets shook, the milk-thistle shook, my hands upon the sill shook with that chaos-mood that is not sadness and is not joy but the trembling that comes before the naming of a thing, before the Spirit lands, and I thought of the God who is not this and not that, not the hawk though the hawk is beautiful, not the thistle though the thistle wounds, not the green line falling on the screen at 9:41 nor the red, not any predicate we hang upon Him like ribbons on a spike, for He is the vertigo behind the numbers, the dark cloud into which the mystics climb backwards, unknowing, and the whole unstable morning was a via negativa written in feathers and thorns and the unspellable name of a company dissolving at the open, MicroSystems, micro-cosmos, small orders collapsing into smaller, the hawk stooping, the thistledown loosed and scattering silver across the Pentecost wind that fills the house and fills nothing, that is present as absence, that says I am not here in any place you'd look, and still the down drifts, still the stock ticks its jittering apophasis down toward zero, that holy number, that rounded nothing which is fuller than all fullness, and I could not tell you if the fire had come or gone, only that the thistles held their purple crowns above the ruin and the hawks did not descend and did not need to, being already, like the God who is no-thing, everywhere unsaid above the shaking, shaking, unaccountable ground.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a piece of modernist poetry that juxtaposes global currencies (dollars, yen, rand, rupees) with a field of red and green thistles, and questions why the speaker can't find emotional balance.
counterfactuals.output:
# Ledger of Thistles

Dollars in the eastern light—
green as the stalk before it splits,
yen folding into yen,
paper cranes that never learned to land.

The rand, the rupee, the small coins
of some accounting I keep
in a pocket with a hole in it.

*Why can't I balance?*

Here: a field.
Red thistles, green thistles,
the arithmetic of a hillside
that owes nothing, tallies nothing,
spends its purple heads to the wind
and calls it profit.

I have converted grief into three markets.
I have hedged the heart against itself.

The exchange rate of a Tuesday—
what is it worth,
this trembling in the wrists,
this red that will not settle into green,
this green that spikes back into red?

Somewhere a bell rings, closing.
Somewhere the thistles do not close,
do not open,
simply *are*,
prickling the ledger
where my name should sum to zero

and does not,
and does not,
and does not.

—

The bank of the body
holds no reserve.
I stand in the field counting
what cannot be counted:
the interest on a wound,
the currency of standing still

while the thistles,
red, green, red,
appreciate
in a light
that asks nothing back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write in the style of a contemporary confessional poet contemplating financial addiction, apocalypse, and utopian longing while standing on a summit road overlooking the sea.
counterfactuals.output:
# Summit Road, Facing the Pacific

I have been reading the market like scripture again,
thumb-scrolling the little green and red gods
into my palm at four in the morning,
that blue light the only prayer I answer.

Below me the sea does what it has always done—
forgives nothing, remembers nothing,
throws its whole silver body at the rocks
and calls it living.

I used to think the end would announce itself.
Trumpet, or at least a headline.
Instead it comes like this: a slow leak,
a number that will not stop meaning something.
I have mortgaged my mornings to a chart.
I have called it *discipline.* I have called it *hope.*

*                    *

Confession: I want the crash.
Not the small one that ruins me,
but the great cleansing zero
that would make the counting stop,
that would leave us blinking on the hillside
with nothing but our hands and this astonishing light,
learning again what a peach costs,
what an hour is worth when no one's buying.

*                    *

There's a version of us up ahead—
I can almost see it from this altitude—
where we put down the ledgers
and the fires and the endless liquid want,
where a road is just a way to somewhere
and not a metaphor for the exit.
Where the word *enough* is not a threat
but a low tide you can walk out into,
the water warm, the shells all yours,
free, because the idea of *yours* has finally drowned.

*                    *

But the phone is warm in my pocket, insistent,
a small animal that needs me.
The sun is doing something extravagant and doomed
across the water, spending itself,
the only creditor I trust,
and I stand here, addicted to the ache
between the world that's ending
and the one I keep almost deserving,

counting the waves the way I count my losses—
each one arriving, each one gone,
the whole horizon promising, promising,
and never once cashing out.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a fragmented, philosophical prose poem where a day-trader on a mountaintop reflects on Götterdämmerung, free radicals, longevity, and his volatile spike-of-chaos temperament.
counterfactuals.output:
# Twilight of the Gods, Quarterly Report

*

I stand where the air thins to almost-nothing, where the market cannot reach me—and yet it reaches me. The candles rise and fall in my chest. Red, green. The oxidation of desire.

*

Wagner understood: the gods burn not from enemies but from *contracts*. Every rope of gold woven becomes the rope that hangs the weaver. I have signed things. I have leveraged the mountain against the valley of my own attention.

*

*Free radicals*—

An electron missing its partner, roaming the cell, taking what it needs from whatever is nearest. I recognize this. I am a molecule with an unpaired want. I steal stability from the tissues around me. I age myself in flashes.

*

Consider the longevity I chase: cold plunges, fasting windows, the supplement that arrives in amber glass. I want to live forever *and* I want to feel the spike—the god-hormone flood when the position breaks my way. These cannot both be true. The chaos that thrills me is the same chaos fraying my telomeres like cheap rope at the end.

*

Valhalla was a portfolio. Diversified across giants and gold and the labor of the dead. It still burned.

*

At altitude the heart works harder for less. I am optimizing. I am dying at a slower rate in order to die suddenly. There is a joke in here that only my cardiologist finds funny.

*

The temperament: I am calm the way a fault line is calm. Someone once said I contained *weather*. When the number moves I do not decide to react—the reaction has already happened somewhere below language, in the old brain, the reptile counting-house.

*

*Antioxidant*, they say. As if a man could simply *donate* an electron to his own hunger and become whole. As if peace were a molecule you could swallow.

*

The Rhine gives back the gold at the end. Everything returns to the river that is indifferent to who held it. My gains, my losses, my mitochondria spilling their small fires—all of it, downstream.

*

Here is what the mountain teaches, which is nothing, which is everything: *I* am the free radical. I am the missing electron of my own life, reaching, oxidizing, glorious and corrosive, unwilling to be stabilized because stability, to me, has always looked too much like death—

*

and the twilight comes for the gods precisely *because* they cannot stop trading.

*

The sun sets. My phone glows. Somewhere a bell.

I press *buy*.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
